claims.text: Annealing a plasma-sprayed HEA coating on Q235 steel promotes diffusion of HEA elements into the steel surface.
Interfacial diffusion produces an oxide scale enriched in protective HEA constituents.
The resulting oxide scale is stable and oxidation-resistant.
The oxide scale acts as a physical and chemical barrier to aggressive salt-induced corrosion.
High temperature increases diffusion kinetics and facilitates formation of a coherent, protective oxide scale.
At room temperature, limited kinetic activation restricts formation and protective quality of the oxide scale.
Under aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C, annealed HEA-coated Q235 steel will have lower mass change than uncoated or non-annealed HEA-coated Q235 steel.
Under aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C, annealed HEA-coated Q235 steel will have lower corrosion-pit density than uncoated or non-annealed HEA-coated Q235 steel.
Under aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C, annealed HEA-coated Q235 steel will exhibit improved overall corrosion resistance relative to both reference conditions.
At room temperature, the corrosion-protection benefit of annealing the HEA coating will be less pronounced or negligible.
The proposed protection mechanism requires enough thermal energy for interdiffusion and oxide-scale stabilization.
Minor coating defects may affect the overall corrosion performance.
A three-group comparison of uncoated, as-sprayed HEA-coated, and annealed HEA-coated Q235 specimens can isolate the effect of coating and annealing.
Failure of the annealed HEA-coated specimens to show statistically significant reductions in mass change or pit density at high temperature would falsify the predicted protection.
Protection at room temperature comparable to that at high temperature would falsify the proposed temperature-dependent mechanism.
